chapter_theme: Natrinai 221-240: homecoming and departure set against the seasons (the son who calls his father, the clouds like a patron's elephants, the cloud that is not noble), the friend's pressure for marriage through gossip, seclusion and the night tryst, and the woman's maxims against wealth-seeking.

comparisons.tenor: the konrai clusters hanging from the boughs
the red-soil forest edge spread with flowers

221.reading: His task done, the man tells his charioteer to drive the long chariot through the red-soil scrub, where karuvilai blue as a gem and bright thondri deck the bushes and konrai clusters hang like gold chains from every bough, so that he may hear the sweet words of his little son, newly walking on untried feet, who leaves his bed and cries 'come, father', in the shining house of his wife who loves to receive guests.
221.nuance: The reward he drives toward is not first the wife but the household she keeps, hospitable and now with a child who has just learned to call him; the flowering season tells him he is already late.

colophon.thurai: வினை முற்றி மறுத்தராநின்ற தலைமகன் பாகற்குச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the konrai and thondri of the rainy forest edge on the road home

iraicchi.act: the tusker trumpets because the mist hides his mate, who sleeps right beside him
iraicchi.sense: once the girl is shut in the house she will be near yet out of his sight, and the man will cry out like the tusker unless he marries her

comparisons.tenor: the girl rising on the swing

222.reading: The friend, knowing the man stands near, asks the girl whether she should push her today on the swing hung from the bent red-flowered vengai branch, its twisted rope scarring the bark, so that she, holding her girdle of green beads, may rise like a peacock playing in the sky and see his far tall hill, where on the slope of plantain, wazhai and bamboo the great tusker, unable to see his mate asleep beside him when the mist comes down, trumpets.
222.nuance: 'Today' is the edge: the girl is about to be kept indoors, so this is the last swing and the last sight of his hill, and the man listening is told so without being addressed.

colophon.thurai: தோழி தலைமகன் வரவு உணர்ந்து சிறைப்புறமாகச் செறிப்பு அறிவுறீஇ வரைவு கடாயது

thinai_evidence.note: vengai, hill slope and tusker of the mountain

223.reading: The friend tells the man of the shore that because the girl's desire is great she forgets it is daytime, and because his love is great he comes even by day to the flower-filled grove; that is sweet, but gossip will have her strictly guarded, so let him come at night instead, except that this gossiping town has women whose eyes never sleep even at the ford of the wide sea where shark shoals teem.
223.nuance: The offer of a night tryst is withdrawn in the same breath: neither day nor night is safe, so the only road left is marriage, which is what the friend wants him to hear.

colophon.thurai: பகற்குறி வந்து மீள்வானைத் தோழி இரவுக்குறி நேர்வாள் போன்று அதுவும் மறுத்து வரைவு கடாயது

thinai_evidence.note: the shore grove, the ford and the sharks of the sea

occasion.words: இரவுக்குறி நேர்வாள் போன்று அதுவும் மறுத்து வரைவு கடாயது

224.reading: Told by her friend that he is leaving, the woman says: they are loving, and great besides; yet the kuravu has budded ahead of the late dew, the red-eyed koel calls from the clusters as if saying 'you who are joined, stay joined', and sweet spring has come to us; what can I say now to those who assured me 'we will not part' and have set their minds on the hot hard waste of dried pools and withered trees where bowmen swarm at the forks?
224.nuance: Her praise of him (loving, great) is what makes argument impossible: she cannot accuse, only set his promise against a season that is itself pleading for union.

colophon.thurai: தோழியால் பிரிவு உணர்த்தப்பட்ட தலைமகள் பெயர்த்தும் சொல் கடாவப்பட்டு அறிவிலாதேம் என்னை சொல்லியும் பிரியார் ஆகாரோ என்று சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the man is setting out across the waste

comparisons.tenor: the bud swaying with its flower

225.reading: The woman asks her friend whether anyone has had to beg the lord of the great mountain, where the plantain's swollen bud, like the white tusk of an elephant that fought in fury with Murugan's strength, sways with its flower like the loose hair of soft women, for the chest without kindness that will not help those who love it, so as to cure the pain that has risen and ruined the drawn lines of her breasts.
225.nuance: The question is bitter: a help that has to be begged for is no help, so she refuses the friend's comfort by asking whether any lover should need to plead.

colophon.thurai: வன்புறை எதிர் அழிந்தது பரத்தை தலைமகட்குப் பாங்காயின வாயில் கேட்பச் சொல்லியதூஉம் ஆம்

thinai_evidence.note: the mountain lord, the hill plantain and the tusker

thurai_akam.speaker: parathai

occasion.words: பரத்தை தலைமகட்குப் பாங்காயின வாயில் கேட்பச் சொல்லியதூஉம்

thurai_akam.note: the courtesan speaks to her own company so that the heroine's go-betweens overhear

comparisons.tenor: the lover who seeks wealth at the cost of the wife who lives by him

226.reading: Answering comfort, the woman says that people do not take a medicine that kills the tree, the great do not do a penance that kills their strength, and kings do not take gold that ruins the land's wealth; yet since our life hangs on his, our lover, not knowing the measure of the wealth he goes to make, has gone over the long scorched way and left us, and the whole world knows it is always so.
226.nuance: Each maxim is about taking from a source without destroying it; she makes herself the source he is draining, so the proverbs of the wise become the charge against him.

thinai_evidence.note: the summer heat on the long way he took

comparisons.vehicle: ஆர்க்காட்டு ஆங்கண் கள்ளுடைத் தடவில் புள் ஒலித்து ஓவாத் தேர் வழங்கு தெருவின்

227.reading: The friend tells the man that worse than losing precious life is to have the wise say one lacks virtue, and yet, alas, his grace to her friend of long thick hair, who met him at the tryst in the punnai grove, has become talk as loud as the streets of the Cholas' Arkkadu, with its belled elephants and banners, where birds cry without stop by the toddy vats and chariots ply.
227.nuance: 'Your grace' is the sting: what he gave as kindness has turned into the town's noise, and only marriage turns it back into virtue.

colophon.thurai: வரையாது நெடுங்காலம் வந்து ஒழுக தோழி தலைமகனை வரைவு முடுகச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the punnai grove of the shore as the trysting place

228.reading: The friend, speaking to the girl so that the man nearby hears, asks what it can mean that on a midnight of thick darkness, when lightning splits the thundering clouds and they pour out their full load, the lord of the mountain of leaping falls, where the great tusker, startled by the arrow shot from the hunter's fierce bow, slides into a crevice and its cry echoes, comes by the cruel hard path: is it that he has no pity for us?
228.nuance: Her fear is for him, not of him: his coming through the night's dangers is called pitiless because it puts the girl through terror, which is the friend's way of urging marriage. The elephant falling into the cleft may be read as the danger awaiting the man, but no second correspondence is stated, so it is left as scene.

colophon.thurai: தோழி சிறைப்புறமாகத் தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய் தலைமகன் கேட்பச் சொல்லியது

occasion.words: சிறைப்புறமாகத் தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய் தலைமகன் கேட்பச் சொல்லியது

229.reading: Told by the man that he is leaving, the friend says: since you keep saying 'we go, we go', I fear to sulk and say 'go', and if I say 'do not go' I fear the petty words of many that wound; so go, go and finish the work, but once there do not linger, for she trembles alone at midnight even when you are near after an embrace that marks her jewelled breast; and have you seen that the north wind has already come and stands here, after the young rains that played coolly where the clouds gathered?
229.nuance: Her consent is made of two fears, and its last line undoes it: the cold wind that has already come is the season in which no man should be away, so the permission ends as a plea to stay, which is why the colophon gives the alternative reading that she held him back.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகனால் பிரிவு உணர்த்தப்பட்ட தோழி தலைமகளை ஆற்றுவித்துச் செல்ல உடன்பட்டது செலவு அழுங்குவித்ததூஉம் ஆம்

thinai_evidence.note: the man's departure for his work

comparisons.vehicle: புதுவறம்கூர்ந்த செறுவில் தண்ணென மலி புனல் பரத்தந்தாஅங்கு
comparisons.tenor: the sight of the man ending her loneliness

230.reading: Refusing the man entry, the friend says in the wife's voice: lord of the town with ponds full of carp, where the cool water-lily, its green leaves like a young she-elephant's ears and its closed buds like a flock of herons, opens smelling of nectar as the morning star rises in the east and the dark goes, you left me for a tireless courtesan and showed no grace; how sweet it is to see you, like a full flood spreading coolly over a field gripped by fresh drought, ending the loneliness that tormented me.
230.nuance: The flood simile can be heard straight or as irony: so rarely does he come that his sight is like rain on a parched field, which is itself the reproach that keeps the door shut.

thinai_evidence.note: the courtesan and the lord of the pond town

comparisons.tenor: the small white crows on the dark sea

231.reading: The friend, with the man within hearing, tells the girl that the shore where many small white crows play, dipping their dark backs in the wide sea like the seven stars worshipped by custom in the spotless sapphire sky, is now desolate, though before it was such that the love given by the lord of the grove of black-trunked punnai, whose big blossoms open like sparrows' eggs broken in the inner town, never left us.
231.nuance: The playful crows in company make the shore's emptiness sharper; the friend recalls the old love only to say that the place where it lived is now lonely, so the man must marry to restore it.

thinai_evidence.note: crows of the sea, punnai of the shore and the shore lord

ullurai.tenor: the man who comes by day close to the girl's house

pairs.situation: he is no longer content with meetings in the grove by day
his coming near the village sets the household and the town in alarm

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the elephant herd of the kurinji hill in a kurinji poem (porul 7.27)

232.reading: The friend tells the man who comes by day: lord of the great mountain, where a herd of small-eyed, great-trunked elephants muddies the cool pool of wild jasmine, tires of the grove's plantains and eats the sweet fruit of the red-stemmed jackfruit beside the bamboo-fenced village while the village cries out, we beg you to grant her love; long may you live, our lord, if you stay the night and go from our stony hamlet, whose courtyard is strewn with fallen vengai blossom.
232.nuance: The elephants that leave the grove for the village's own trees and set it crying are what his daytime visits look like from the house: the request to come by night and lodge in the hamlet is a step toward being received there openly.

colophon.thurai: பகல் வருவானை இரவு வா எனத் தோழி சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: elephants, vengai and the mountain lord

233.reading: The friend, so that the man nearby hears, tells the girl who suffers from the long unmarried visits: if you have given your grace to the lord of the great rocky land, where on the high slope the sturdy young of the female monkey, whose untaught male trembles, hides in the drifting cloud, why will you not take my word? I say one plain thing: be sure that he is a worthy man who keeps the tenderness of a kind heart and does not stray from the path the wise have walked.
233.nuance: Praise is pressure: by calling him one who walks the path of the wise in his hearing, the friend makes delay a breach of that path. The trembling monkey and the hidden young may hint at the anxious family, but only one correspondence is clear, so no ullurai is tagged.

colophon.thurai: வரையாது நெடுங்காலம் வந்து ஒழுக இவள் ஆற்றாள் என்பது உணர்ந்து சிறைப் புறமாகத் தலைமகட்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the monkeys of the high slope

235.reading: The friend tells the girl that though the lord of the long waters came to the day tryst in the shore grove where the saw-edged, thorny-leaved thaazhai on the wave-beaten rough trunk and the gold-pollened punnai give off their scent together, and left so that her beauty wasted, they should now climb the heaped dune that rises like a hill and watch the road by which he will come, bees humming over the cool garland on his chest, driving his proud horses with ringing bells.
235.nuance: The grievance and the joy are in one sentence: the wasting he caused is admitted, then set aside for the sight of him arriving with the full show of a bridegroom.

colophon.thurai: வரைவு நீட ஆற்றாளாங் காலத்துத் தோழி வரைவு மலிந்தது

thinai_evidence.note: thaazhai, punnai and the dunes of the shore

236.reading: The woman tells her friend, with the man standing by: my sickness is past bearing and my body burns as if spitting fire; so go and tell my mother of the hellish heart that if I am let out into the courtyard to breathe a little I will recover much, for a little while ago the wind that played on the tall peak of the hill of him who loosened my fine bright bangles, and plunged into its wide rock pools, touched my pale body and cooled it.
236.nuance: Only she and the overhearing man know why the courtyard would heal her: the wind comes from his hill, so her cure is to be nearer him, which is a plea to him to come.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறமாக வற்புறுக்கும் தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: his hill, its peak and rock pools

comparisons.tenor: the dark rain clouds of many shapes

237.reading: The friend asks the girl, her shoulders pale and shrunken and her eyes full of tears as never before, whether she has no sulk at all against the lover dear as life who has left and stays away; look there, she says, the rain clouds of many shapes beyond telling are rising high and wonderful so that the world rejoices, like the elephants Andiran gathered when he undertook to keep the suppliants who come to him.
237.nuance: The friend turns from grief to a sign: the clouds rise like a patron's gift laid up for those who ask, so the season itself promises that what is owed will come, and the girl's sulk can wait for him.

thinai_evidence.note: the rains rising while she waits for the man who stays away

comparisons.vehicle: குறும் பூங் கோதை மகளிர் குழூஉ நிரை

comparisons.tenor: the cloud (denied: it does not behave like the noble)

238.reading: Seeing the season, the woman reproaches the great cloud: in the forest the drought had killed, the pidavam has opened as bees part it, like rows of women wearing short flower garlands, and you, cloud that brings the season along the dim paths of evening, come here as if asking whether I know where he is; that is not how the noble behave; and besides dulling the hoods of snakes in the water spread by the roaring thunder, even to a heart that has not softened your thundering voice is not sweet.
238.nuance: She judges the cloud by the conduct of the noble, who would not torment a woman alone; the season that should mean his return arrives as an insult because he has not.

thinai_evidence.note: the pidavam, evening and the season's rain

239.reading: The friend, with the man within hearing, says: as the setting sun hides behind the western hill in the dimming evening, the glad fishermen easily trade the great fish they caught and, on the way to their lovely hamlet with its fish-smelling sandy yard where crabs play, trample the neythal flowers whose dull petals unwrap like a bundle of fine gems; we have not even agreed to hear of the shore lord's suit, and yet this town has stirred up talk as if he had pulled my friend's bright bangles till they broke, saying 'embrace'; what would it make of it if we did something more?
239.nuance: The fishermen treading down the flowers on their careless way home have been read as the man's carelessness of her, but the pairs are not secure; the poem's point is that gossip already runs ahead of any deed, so he must act to make it true by marrying.

thinai_evidence.note: fishermen, neythal flowers and crabs of the shore at sunset

comparisons.tenor: the forest road he must cross

240.reading: Pushed by his heart toward wealth, the man says: how strange is the one who made this world! though the embrace of the young girl with fine sharp white teeth and bright brow, her arms clasping, body pressed and twisting, her swelling breast heaving, is such that sleep can come between us, still the forest, where at the well dug with picks in a pebbled hollow sheltered from the burning sun the elephant herd seizes the trough the herders dug for the cattle, stands before me like a firm mountain.
240.nuance: He knows even the closest embrace has gaps, and that is the excuse the heart uses; but the road, where even the herders' water is taken by elephants, is the obstacle he cannot argue away. The colophon also gives the lines to the heroine wasting in separation.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவிடை மெலிந்த தலைமகள் சொல்லியது நெஞ்சினால் பொருள் வலிக்கப்பட்டு ஆற்றானாய தலைமகன் சொல்லியதூஉம் ஆம்

thinai_evidence.note: the sun-scorched forest where water is dug from wells

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named; likely her friend

links.note: Kural 1268: let the king fight and win, and let me join my home and keep the evening feast. Natrinai 221: the work done, the man bids the charioteer hurry to the wife who loves to host guests and the son who now calls him.
links.teaches: The Kural states the soldier's wish to trade the king's war for the evening feast at home in two lines; the Natrinai scene fills that home with a hospitable wife and a child just learning to walk and call him father, so the 'feast' of the couplet is shown to be a whole household's welcome, not only the wife's.

links.note: Akananuru 374: campaign over, the man bids the chariot go through the morning rains so the slender wife may receive him as a guest. Natrinai 221: the man bids the charioteer go so he may hear his small son's first call to him.
links.teaches: Both homecoming speeches to the charioteer turn on விருந்து, but the Akananuru makes the returning husband the guest his wife receives, while the Natrinai makes the wife the one who loves receiving guests and adds the son, so the convention could place the hero either as guest or as master of a hospitable house.

links.note: Kural 1154: if he who said 'fear not' leaves, is there any fault in those who trusted his assuring word? Natrinai 224: what can I say now to those who assured me 'we will not part' and set off for the waste?
links.teaches: The Kural poses as a moral question who is at fault when an assurance is broken; the Natrinai woman, using the same verb of assuring (தெளித்த), cannot even ask it aloud and lets the budding kuravu and the koel's 'stay joined' do the accusing, so the broken word is judged by the season instead of by her.

links.note: Purananuru 184: a king who takes his due like an elephant fed balls of paddy keeps the land rich, but one who grabs is like an elephant loosed in the field. Natrinai 226: kings do not take gold that ruins the land's wealth, yet her lover does not know the measure of the wealth he seeks.
links.teaches: The counsel that a king must take tribute without ruining its source had become a proverb a wife could quote, and Natrinai 226 turns it on the household: a husband who leaves to make wealth regardless of her life is the elephant loose in the field.

links.note: Kuruntokai 258: the friend says talk has risen on seeing the beauty, like Azhisi's Arkkadu, of this girl wasting. Natrinai 227: the friend says the man's grace has become talk as loud as the streets of the Cholas' Arkkadu.
links.teaches: In two speeches of the same kind, a friend telling the man that gossip has risen, the one town Arkkadu stands once for the girl's endangered beauty and once for the noise of the gossip itself, so a famous town was a measure akam poets could set against either side of the alar.

links.note: Kural 1151: if you are not going, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will be alive then. Natrinai 229: so go, finish the work, but do not linger, for the north wind has come.
links.teaches: Faced with the same announcement of departure, the Kural's speaker refuses any promise of a quick return as useless to the dying, while the Natrinai friend bargains for exactly that promise and binds it to a season already arrived, so two stances to a leaving husband stand side by side: refusal by death, and consent with a deadline.

links.note: Purananuru 133: go and see Ay of the chariots, whose giving is like the rain. Natrinai 237: the rain clouds rise like the elephants Andiran gathered for suppliants.
links.teaches: The puram poet likens Ay's giving to rain, and the akam poet turns it round and likens the rain clouds to Ay's gift elephants, so the patron's bounty and the monsoon were interchangeable images and the friend can offer the season as a promise as sure as a great giver's word.

links.note: Kar Narpathu 12: his coming is certain; every day the dark clouds, like elephants anointed with oil, rise on the right. Natrinai 237: look, the clouds rise like the elephants Andiran gathered.
links.teaches: Both friends point a pining woman to clouds that rise like elephants as proof of the season's return, but Kar Narpathu's anointed elephants and the rising on the right make the cloud an omen, while Natrinai's patron's elephants make it a gift laid up for those who wait, so the same image could reassure by augury or by the ethic of giving.

links.note: Kuruntokai 158: the woman asks the storm cloud, whose thunder strikes snakes on the slopes and can shake the Himalaya, whether it has no pity for women without a companion. Natrinai 238: the woman tells the season's cloud that its coming is not like the noble, and its thunder that dulls the snakes' hoods is not sweet even to a hard heart.
links.teaches: Both women rebuke the thundering cloud of the season, but the Kuruntokai shames it by its might, while the Natrinai holds it to the conduct of the noble (சான்றோர்), so the reproach to the absent man is voiced in one through power misused and in the other through manners breached.

links.note: Kural 1108: sweet to two who desire each other is an embrace that not even a breeze can part. Natrinai 240: even the closest embrace is such that sleep comes between, yet the forest road stands like a mountain.
links.teaches: The Kural makes the gapless embrace the ideal of union; the Natrinai lover admits that even such an embrace is parted by sleep, and that admission is what lets his heart argue for leaving, so the ideal of perfect closeness becomes, in the man's mouth, a reason that union is already imperfect.

source_issues: 234: no text in the core file (the poem is lost); not marked.
225: the colophon files a kurinji poem under an alternative in which the courtesan speaks, a situation of marutham; the alternative is recorded as given.
228 line 6: கானவன் சிறு புறம் கடுக்கும் is obscure; the tusker is read as startled by the hunter's arrow, and the verse is marked uncertain.
233 lines 1 to 5: the sense of மாணா வன் பறழ் ... ஒளிக்கும் and of இனி என கொள்ளலைமன்னே is uncertain; marked uncertain.
238 lines 6 to 10: the construction (அவர் நிலை அறியுமோ ஈங்கு என வருதல்; பாம்பு பை மழுங்கல் அன்றியும்) is uncertain; marked uncertain.
239 lines 9 to 12: who weeps or clamours (கலுழ்ந்த இவ் ஊர்) and the sense of அமைந்து தொழில் கேட்டன்றோ இலமே are uncertain; marked uncertain.
226 lines 4 and 5: நாம் தம் உண்மையின் உளமே and தாம் கசிந்து are read as 'our life rests on his' and 'moved'; uncertain.
229 line 9: குழைவான் கண்ணிடத்து ஈண்டி is obscure; read as clouds gathering low.
237: the poem's rising rain clouds point to mullai against the colophon's paalai.
231 lines 5 to 9: the syntax of பண்டும் ... நீங்காமாறே is uncertain; marked uncertain.
240: the colophon gives two speakers; the reading follows the hero alternative, which the poem's first line and embrace description fit better.
